claim: Tacr1 has been widely used as a marker for projection neurons in the spinal cord.
source: Tacr1 has been widely used as a marker for projection neurons in the spinal cord (Todd, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Todd, 2010

claim: Not all projection neurons are marked by Tacr1.
source: however, not all projection neurons are marked by Tacr1 (Choi et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2020

claim: Interneurons also express Tacr1.
source: and interneurons also express this gene (Sathyamurthy et al., 2020; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sathyamurthy et al., 2020 and 2018

claim: Spinal Tacr1 neurons play a crucial role in normal nociceptive behaviors.
source: Nonetheless, the spinalTacr1 neurons are well known to play a crucial role in normal nociceptive behaviors (Mantyh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mantyh et al., 1997

claim: About 40% of Tacr1Cre-targeted neurons have soma diameters characteristic of projection neurons.
source: Our results confirmed that Tacr1Cre mediates recombination both in the superficial and deep dorsal horn with about 40% of targeted neurons having soma diameters of projection neurons (Al Ghamdi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and citation to Al Ghamdi et al., 2009

claim: Tacr1Cre mediates recombination in both superficial and deep dorsal horn.
source: Our results confirmed that Tacr1Cre mediates recombination both in the superficial and deep dorsal horn with about 40% of targeted neurons having soma diameters of projection neurons (Al Ghamdi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Administration of CNO to mice with hM3Dq-expressing spinal Tacr1 neurons results in widespread Fos expression on the injected side.
source: Importantly, administration of the hM3Dq ligand clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) resulted in widespread Fos expression on the injected side (Figure 1B), validating this stimulation paradigm (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B for quantitation).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Both hM3Dq-mCherry positive and negative neurons express Fos after CNO delivery.
source: Our results showed that both hM3Dq-mCherry positive and negative neurons express Fos after CNO delivery.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: CNO activates Tacr1+ neurons, which in turn activate other non-Tacr1 neurons.
source: A likely explanation is that CNO activates Tacr1+ neurons, and that Tacr1+ neurons in turn activate other non-Tacr1 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from observation that both mCherry+ and mCherry- neurons express Fos

claim: Each side of a lumbar spinal cord segment receives sensory inputs from the ipsilateral hindlimb.
source: Each side of a lumbar spinal cord segment receives sensory inputs from the ipsilateral hindlimb (Basbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basbaum et al., 2009

claim: Within minutes of CNO application, animals with spinal Tacr1 neurons expressing hM3Dq began spontaneously lifting, shaking and licking the hindlimb ipsilateral to the AAV injection.
source: Within minutes of CNO application, animals with spinalTacr1 neurons expressing hM3Dq began spontaneously lifting, shaking and licking the hindlimb ipsilateral to the AAV injection (Figure 1C and D; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1C, D and Videos 1 and 2

claim: The responses evoked by CNO activation of spinal Tacr1 neurons were highly reminiscent of those caused by extremely noxious and persistent stimuli such as chemical irritants.
source: These responses were highly reminiscent of those caused by extremely noxious and persistent stimuli such as chemical irritants (Kwan et al., 2006)
evidence: Comparison to known responses from literature, supported by citation to Kwan et al., 2006

claim: CNO-induced behaviors in mice with hM3Dq-expressing spinal Tacr1 neurons lasted for over an hour.
source: These responses were highly reminiscent of those caused by extremely noxious and persistent stimuli such as chemical irritants (Kwan et al., 2006), lasted for over an hour and suppressed normal homecage behaviors (e.g. grooming; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation and data in Figure 1E

claim: CNO-induced activation of spinal Tacr1 neurons suppressed normal grooming behaviors.
source: These responses were highly reminiscent of those caused by extremely noxious and persistent stimuli such as chemical irritants (Kwan et al., 2006), lasted for over an hour and suppressed normal homecage behaviors (e.g. grooming; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1E

claim: Animals with CNO-activated spinal Tacr1 neurons were completely unresponsive to chloroquine, a potent puritogen.
source: Remarkably, animals on CNO became so focused on the DREADD-induced 'fictive' pain associated with the ipsilateral hindlimb that they ignored other highly salient stimuli. In particular, they were completely unresponsive to chloroquine, a potent puritogen (Han et al., 2013; Mishra and Hoon, 2013) that normally causes robust and long-lasting scratching (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1F and citations to Han et al., 2013 and Mishra and Hoon, 2013

claim: Chloroquine was applied to the nape of the neck, a completely different body area from the hindlimb.
source: Notably, chloroquine was applied to the nape of the neck, a completely different body area, and still induced Fos expression in the cervical spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental description and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Chloroquine application to the nape of the neck induced Fos expression in the cervical spinal cord.
source: Notably, chloroquine was applied to the nape of the neck, a completely different body area, and still induced Fos expression in the cervical spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Activation of a small group of lumbar spinal Tacr1 neurons produced the phenomenon of itch suppression by pain.
source: Thus, in addition to directing nocifensive behavior to a somatotopically conscribed area, the activation of a small group of lumbar spinalTacr1 neurons produced the well-known phenomenon of itch suppression by pain (Ikoma et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data and supported by citation to Ikoma et al., 2006

claim: Itch suppression by pain involves a central mechanism since peripheral signaling persists.
source: Moreover, our data strongly suggest that itch suppression by pain must involve a central mechanism since peripheral signaling persists.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that chloroquine still induces Fos in cervical spinal cord despite suppressed scratching

claim: The effects of CNO on spinal Tacr1 neuron activation were fully reversible and did not cause any long-lasting sensitization.
source: Finally, as expected, the effects of CNO were fully reversible and did not cause any long-lasting sensitization (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1G and H showing normal thresholds 24 hours post-CNO

claim: Ablating spinal neurons expressing Tac1 significantly impaired licking responses to sustained noxious stimuli.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that ablating spinal neurons expressing Tac1, the gene encoding the neuropeptide Substance P, significantly impaired licking responses to sustained noxious stimuli (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huang et al., 2019

claim: In the spinal cord, Tac1 is broadly expressed both in projection neurons and interneurons.
source: In the spinal cord, Tac1 is also broadly expressed both in projection neurons and interneurons (Gutierrez-Mecinas et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gutierrez-Mecinas et al., 2017 and Huang et al., 2019

claim: Cells with high levels of Tacr1 transcripts in the superficial dorsal horn almost always co-express Tac1.
source: Our in-situ hybridization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B) revealed cells with high levels of Tacr1 transcripts in the superficial dorsal horn almost always co-express Tac1.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinal Tac1 neurons resulted in robust nocifensive behaviors directed to the ipsilateral hindlimb.
source: As predicted, chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinalTac1 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, E) resulted in robust nocifensive behaviors directed to the ipsilateral hindlimb while at the same time suppressing grooming (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F) and itch responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, E, F, G

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinal Tac1 neurons suppressed grooming behaviors.
source: As predicted, chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinalTac1 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, E) resulted in robust nocifensive behaviors directed to the ipsilateral hindlimb while at the same time suppressing grooming (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F) and itch responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinal Tac1 neurons suppressed itch responses.
source: As predicted, chemogenetic stimulation of lumbar spinalTac1 neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, E) resulted in robust nocifensive behaviors directed to the ipsilateral hindlimb while at the same time suppressing grooming (Figure 1—figure supplement 4F) and itch responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 4G).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4G

claim: Stimulation of Tac1Cre animals produced more robust behaviors than stimulation of Tacr1Cre mice.
source: There were minor differences in the behaviors with stimulation of Tac1Cre animals being more robust than Tacr1Cre mice (compare Videos 2 and 3), perhaps in part due to activation of Tac1 (Substance P but not NKR1) expressing sensory neurons in the dorsal horn and dorsal root ganglion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4H).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Videos 2 and 3 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4H

claim: Activity of spinal cells expressing Tac1 and Tacr1 carries the information needed to elicit a pain sensation localized to a specific body area.
source: Importantly, our results demonstrate that activity of the spinal cells expressing these genes carries the information needed to elicit a pain sensation localized to a specific body area.
evidence: Inferred from the somatotopic behavioral responses observed with chemogenetic activation

claim: Pain has many dimensions including location, quality, intensity, and duration.
source: Pain has many dimensions including location, quality, intensity, and duration.
evidence: Established knowledge about pain

claim: Pain affects physiology, emotion, attention, and memory.
source: It also affects physiology, emotion, attention, and memory (Bushnell et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bushnell et al., 2013

claim: Output from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord targets multiple brain areas that work in concert to generate pain.
source: Output from the dorsal horn of the spinal cord targets multiple brain areas that work in concert to generate this complex state (Basbaum et al., 2009; Todd, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Basbaum et al., 2009 and Todd, 2010

claim: Anterograde tracing of spinal Tacr1 neurons revealed GFP+ axons in many regions of the brain.
source: Consistent with their ability to coordinate a full-blown pain response, anterograde tracing revealed GFP+ axons in many regions of the brain (Figure 1J-M).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data in Figure 1J-M

claim: The highest density of spinal Tacr1 projections was at the very top of the superior lateral PBN (PBN-SL).
source: Although GFP+ axons targeted both these regions, the highest density of spinalTacr1 projections was at the very top of the superior lateral PBN (PBN-SL; Figure 1K), a small and anatomically distinct area with unknown function and is sometimes referred to as the internal lateral PBN (Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data in Figure 1K and citation to Choi et al., 2020

claim: Chemogenetic activation of spinal Tacr1 neurons induced robust Fos expression in the PBN-SL.
source: As expected, chemogenetic activation of spinalTacr1 (Figure 2A) and spinalTac1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4I) neurons induced robust Fos expression in the PBN-SL.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4I

claim: Tacr1 is highly expressed in a tight cluster of excitatory cells in the PBN-SL.
source: Indeed, multiplex fluorescent in-situ hybridization revealed Tacr1 to be highly expressed in a tight cluster of excitatory cells in the PBN-SL (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Most Tacr1-positive PBN-SL neurons are glutamatergic.
source: Co-staining for the glutamate vesicular transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2; cyan) and GABA vesicular transporter SLC32A1 (Vgat; green) reveals most Tacr1-positive PBN-SL neurons are glutamatergic and hence excitatory.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 2B, C

claim: Near super-resolution imaging showed very close apposition of spinal Tacr1 presynaptic specializations and PBN-SL Tacr1 postsynaptic specializations indicative of functional synapses.
source: Near super-resolution imaging of single Z planes from stained tissue sections from the PBN-SL showed very close apposition of red and green varicosities indicative of functional synapses (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by Airyscan imaging data in Figure 2F, G

claim: The majority of spinal Tacr1 projection neurons target PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons.
source: Quantification of number of SypYFP puncta with PSD95tagRFP puncta in close apposition (left graph) and vice versa (right graph) demonstrate that the majority of spinal projection neurons target PBN-SLTacr1 neurons; n = 7 sections from n = 3 mice.
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2G

claim: Two forebrain regions were prominently innervated by PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons: the midline thalamus (MTh) and the lateral hypothalamus/parasubthalamic nucleus (LH/PSTN).
source: Two forebrain regions were prominently innervated by PBN-SLTacr1 neurons (Figure 2J): (1) the midline thalamus (MTh) and (2) the lateral hypothalamus/ parasubthalamic nucleus (LH/PSTN).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data in Figure 2J

claim: MTh and LH/PSTN appear to be selective targets of PBN-SL excitatory projections that are not innervated by other lateral PBN subnuclei.
source: Both these regions appear to be selective targets of PBN-SL excitatory projections that are not innervated by other lateral PBN subnuclei (Barik et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barik et al., 2018

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons that project to LH/PSTN also have collaterals that make presynaptic terminal specializations in the MTh.
source: Importantly, Synaptophysin-GFP puncta were also abundant in the MTh (Figure 3B) demonstrating collateralization of PBN cells that we presume express Tacr1.
evidence: Supported by intersectional tracing data in Figure 3B

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons exhibited robust population calcium responses to sustained mechanical stimulation.
source: Again, PBN-SLTacr1 neurons exhibited robust population calcium responses to this type of stimulation (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4D, E

claim: Punctate mechanical stimuli did not evoke calcium responses in PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons.
source: By contrast, punctate mechanical stimuli did not evoke calcium responses in PBN-SLTacr1 neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4F

claim: Pinprick failed to evoke a calcium response in PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons.
source: Additionally, pinprick also failed to evoke a calcium response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons preferentially respond to sustained stimuli.
source: Together, these data may indicate that PBN-SLTacr1 neurons preferentially respond to sustained stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the differential responses to sustained vs. acute stimuli

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons exhibited robust activity to hot-plate exposure.
source: In keeping with these neurons playing a general role in pain sensation they exhibited robust activity to hot-plate exposure (Figure 4G)
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4G

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons exhibited robust activity to topical application of AITC.
source: In keeping with these neurons playing a general role in pain sensation they exhibited robust activity to hot-plate exposure (Figure 4G) and topical application of the pungent component of mustard oil, allyl isothiocyanate (AITC; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons were not activated by short-term noxious heat (Hargreaves test).
source: However, PBN-SLTacr1 neurons were not activated by short-term noxious heat (Hargreaves test; Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4H

claim: AITC-induced skin irritation did not sensitize PBN-SL Tacr1 responses to acute touch or heat stimuli.
source: Interestingly, although AITC is known to cause allodynia and hyperalgesia (Albin et al., 2008), this type of skin irritation did not sensitize PBN-SLTacr1 responses to acute touch or heat stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-F).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-F and citation to Albin et al., 2008

claim: Activation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons did not induce spontaneous directed pain responses.
source: Although activation of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons did not induce spontaneous directed pain responses, CNO delivery transformed behavior: mice became skittish, avoided handling and repeatedly attempted to escape from the test chambers (possibly a general pain state).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations

claim: CNO delivery to mice with hM3Dq-expressing PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons caused mice to become skittish, avoid handling and repeatedly attempt to escape from test chambers.
source: Although activation of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons did not induce spontaneous directed pain responses, CNO delivery transformed behavior: mice became skittish, avoided handling and repeatedly attempted to escape from the test chambers (possibly a general pain state).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations

claim: Activation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons resulted in heightened arousal and anxiety quantified as increased movement and avoidance of the center in an open-field arena.
source: This heightened arousal and anxiety were quantified using an open-field arena as increased movement and avoidance of the center (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Mice with activated PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons withdrew from the slightest touch with thin von Frey filaments (0.07 g).
source: Mice now withdrew from the slightest touch with thin von Frey filaments (0.07 g; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), something not seen in saline controls.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Activation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons increased nocifensive behavior and almost doubled the time a mouse spent shaking the clipped paw in the clip assay.
source: Moreover, in a sustained pinch assay using a clip applied to the paw, activation of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons increased nocifensive behavior and almost doubled the time a mouse spent shaking the clipped paw (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5C, D

claim: After clip removal, CNO-treated mice with activated PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons continued to lick and investigate the hindpaw for many minutes.
source: Although saline -treated mice quickly returned to normal resting behaviors, after CNO the same animals continued to lick and investigate the hindpaw for many minutes after the pinch was terminated (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5E

claim: Stimulating PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons more than doubled the time a CNO-treated mouse spent licking the AITC-injected site.
source: Equally robust effects of stimulating PBN-SLTacr1 neurons were observed in responses to AITC, a chemical irritant which normally causes licking and attending to the affected area (Figure 5F). The time a CNO-treated mouse spent licking the injected site more than doubled.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5F

claim: CNO-injected mice with activated PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons exhibited heightened escape responses when exposed to heat in a hotplate assay.
source: CNO-injected mice also exhibited heightened escape responses when exposed to heat in a hotplate assay (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5G

claim: The latency in a mouse's response to heat was not influenced by activation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons, indicating that peripheral sensitization is not involved.
source: Interestingly, the latency in a mouse's response to heat, thought to involve simple spinal reflexes, was not influenced indicating that peripheral sensitization is not involved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Activation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons induces a 'hyper-vigilant' state resembling the effects of long-term noxious stimulation.
source: Thus, activation of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons induces a 'hyper-vigilant' state resembling the effects of long-term noxious stimulation (e.g. inflammation) as seen in assays like the formalin test (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from behavioral observations and comparison to formalin test data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Activating PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons using CNO did not enhance responses to formalin.
source: Interestingly, activating the PBN-SLTacr1 neurons using CNO did not enhance responses to formalin, presumably reflecting the potency of this inflammatory stimulus.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Inhibiting PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons reduces behavioral responses to peripheral inflammation.
source: In a related study, the Sun lab has demonstrated that inhibiting PBN-SLTacr1 neurons reduces behavioral responses to peripheral inflammation (Deng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deng et al., 2020

claim: Chemogenetic stimulation of PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons completely suppressed scratching induced by chloroquine.
source: Remarkably, chemogenetic stimulation of the small group of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons completely suppressed scratching (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons serve as a central substrate that is sufficient to suppress itch.
source: Therefore, the PBN-SLTacr1 neurons serve as a central substrate that is sufficient to suppress itch.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that activating these neurons suppresses scratching

claim: Silencing PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons almost completely eliminated shaking and licking normally induced by the clip assay and topical application of AITC.
source: Remarkably, in both cases, silencing PBN-SLTacr1 neurons almost completely eliminated shaking and licking normally induced by these stimuli (Figure 5K–O).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5K-O

claim: Mice with silenced PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons effectively ignored normally painful stimuli.
source: Moreover, at a qualitative level, mice with silenced PBN-SLTacr1 neurons effectively ignored these normally painful stimuli.
evidence: Qualitative behavioral observation

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons play a profound role in pain and are necessary for normal behavioral responses.
source: Thus, this small and localized cluster of PBN-SLTacr1 neurons appears to play a profound role in pain and is necessary for normal behavioral responses.
evidence: Inferred from the silencing experiments showing loss of pain behaviors

claim: A circuit involving Tacr1-expressing neurons in the spinal cord and the PBN-SL controls how mice respond to a wide range of persistently painful stimuli.
source: Together our results identify a circuit involving Tacr1-expressing neurons in the spinal cord and the PBN-SL that controls how mice respond to a wide range of persistently painful stimuli.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: More than 30 years ago McMahon and Wall described a loop from lamina I dorsal horn to the parabrachial nucleus that influences the activity of lamina I cells.
source: Interestingly, more than 30 years ago McMahon and Wall described a loop from lamina I dorsal horn to the parabrachial nucleus that influences the activity of lamina I cells (McMahon and Wall, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to McMahon and Wall, 1988

claim: PBN-SL neurons expressing Tacr1 are important for responses to persistent noxious stimuli.
source: Our results here show that PBN-SL neurons expressing Tacr1 are important for responses to persistent noxious stimuli, exactly as predicted (Wall et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by experimental findings and citation to Wall et al., 1988

claim: Spinal Tacr1 neurons are quite diverse.
source: Very recently and in keeping with our data, other groups have demonstrated that spinalTacr1 neurons are quite diverse (Sheahan et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Sheahan et al., 2020 and Choi et al., 2020

claim: Spinal Tacr1 neurons include a population that selectively innervates the PBN-SL to cause strong nocifensive responses.
source: Very recently and in keeping with our data, other groups have demonstrated that spinalTacr1 neurons are quite diverse (Sheahan et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2020) and include a population of neurons that selectively innervate the PBN-SL to cause strong nocifensive responses (Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2020

claim: Chemogenetic activation of spinal Tacr1 neurons using a different genetic strategy induced itch-related behavior.
source: Interestingly, chemogenetic activation of spinalTacr1 neurons using a different genetic strategy induced itch-related behavior (Sheahan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheahan et al., 2020

claim: Different mouse lines and approaches likely targeted slightly different subsets or numbers of neurons to elicit distinct sensations.
source: In combination, these data highlight the role of spinalTacr1 neurons in nociception but suggest that the different mouse lines and approaches likely targeted slightly different subsets or numbers of neurons to elicit distinct sensations.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of results across different studies

claim: A primary target of spinal Tacr1 projection neurons are PBN-SL neurons that also express the NKR1-receptor.
source: We show that a primary target of spinalTacr1 projection neurons are PBN-SL neurons that also express the NKR1-receptor.
evidence: Supported by anatomical and molecular data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons are both necessary and sufficient to drive a subset of pain-related behaviors.
source: These PBN-SLTacr1 neurons are both necessary and sufficient to drive a subset of pain-related behaviors.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic activation and silencing experiments in Figure 5

claim: PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons are tuned to long-lasting noxious input regardless of location.
source: PBN-SLTacr1 neurons are tuned to long-lasting noxious input regardless of location and are selectively important for behaviors that only occur when pain is persistent.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data in Figure 4

claim: When activated, PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons dramatically potentiate complex behavioral responses but not simple reflexes.
source: When activated, PBN-SLTacr1 neurons dramatically potentiate complex behavioral responses but not simple reflexes.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5 showing enhanced complex behaviors but no change in reflex latencies

claim: When PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons are stimulated in the absence of noxious peripheral input, mice become 'jumpy' and hypervigilant.
source: Interestingly, when this group of neurons is stimulated in the absence of noxious peripheral input, mice become 'jumpy' and hypervigilant, now recoiling vigorously from the gentlest of touches that normally would be ignored in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations

claim: Unlike spinal projection neurons, PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons do not themselves evoke pain responses or provide positional information but instead appear to drive affective aspects of pain.
source: Finally, unlike spinal projection neurons, PBN-SLTacr1 neurons do not themselves evoke pain responses or provide positional information but instead appear to drive affective aspects of pain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that activating these neurons alone doesn't cause directed pain behaviors but enhances responses to noxious stimuli

claim: Mice with silenced PBN-SL Tacr1 neurons almost completely ignore sustained, normally painful pinch in the clip assay.
source: This is particularly apparent in the clip assay where mice with silenced PBN-SLTacr1 neurons almost completely ignore this type of sustained, and normally painful, pinch.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5K-M
